newsitem.title: UK: LME copper spread deflates, stocks near key level.
newsitem.headline: LME copper spread deflates, stocks near key level.

text.p: The benchmark LME copper spread narrowed on Tuesday as stocks approached the psychological 200,000-tonne mark, while the other metals went their own way.
Tin edged down to a fresh 2-1/3 year low while zinc chipped away at the upside to record a new seven year peak.
In copper, the premium of cash over three month prices eased to a bid of $80 in a bout of nervous afternoon trading from $150 on Monday evening.
It bounced slightly, however, to be indicated at $100/$110 by the end of the afternoon kerb.
Last week, the cash/threes spread hit a $270 backwardation.
"We've gone past the main areas of tightness, so it is not surprising to see the back return to a more equilibrium level," said analyst William Adams of broker Rudolf Wolff.
In the morning, the market was hit by a stock increase of 11,550 tonnes, which brought total LME inventories to 195,950 tonnes.
Some in the market had believed that Monday's more moderate stocks rise of 3,250 tonnes indicated that last week's large deliveries were one-off occurrences.
The market was rattled as stocks neared the 200,000-tonne level, graphic evidence of metal being sucked in by the backwardation and the impact of the traditionally slow summer period.
As the cash/threes backwardation narrowed, the three months market lost sight of the $2,300 mark, slipping to $2,292, but it pared losses to end the afternoon kerb down $19 at $2,300 per tonne.
Now that the backwardation has lost steam, players will be more inclined to sell into rallies, Adams said.
Zinc kept up its determined climb, achieving another peak of $1,545, a fresh high since August 1990. It ended the day $14 stronger at $1,544.
Prices have ignored overbought signals that have pushed the 14-day RSI to 80.7 and analysts say next targets are $1,550 and $1,600.
The cash/threes spread tightened, ending the day indicated level after a $10/$7 contango on Monday.
On the opposite extreme, tin shuffled to fresh lows since early March 1995, touching a low of $5,360 as hand-to-mouth consumers hold back for lower prices.
Devaluations of South East Asian currencies may have encouraged producers there to sell more metal since they would see gains in domestic terms, analysts said.
Aluminium held above $1,600 after briefly probing below that psychological level to $1,596.
Trade buying kicked in and enabled the market to turn around and skate up to end the day at $1,615, a gain of $6.
Good support has been affirmed around $1,540 and although the market has been having problems breaking higher, the bias is on the upside, Adams said.

Nickel drifted towards the bottom of its recent range after a brief flurry of excitement when Russia's Norilsk Nickel said two of five furnaces at a smelting plant were shut down after a weekend fire.
But when it emerged that little output was immediately affected, prices came off, ending the day $25 weaker at $6,765.
Lead was little changed at $645, down $2, while alloy was indicated at $1,448/53, up $3.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
